title: Write texts for a range of communicative contexts

lessons.title: Planning texts for purpose and audience
lessons.html:
Writing as a team leader

Team leaders in packhouses, poultry plants and seed operations write for many purposes: incident reports, shift handover notes, memos, emails to suppliers, motivations for new equipment, minutes of meetings and simple procedures. Each context needs a different type of text.

The planning questions

  • Purpose: to inform, instruct, request, report, persuade, record?
  • Audience: who will read it and what do they already know? What language level suits them?
  • Context: internal or external? Formal or informal? Urgent or routine?
  • Format: email, memo, letter, report, form, notice, minutes?
  • Content: what facts, figures and examples are needed?

Matching text type to context

ContextText typeStyle
A packer slipped on a wet floorIncident reportFactual, objective, chronological
Asking maintenance to repair a conveyorJob card or emailBrief, specific, includes location and urgency
Requesting a new hand-wash stationMotivation memoPersuasive, supported by facts and costs
Informing all staff about a public holiday shiftNoticeShort, clear, large heading, key details
Recording a production meetingMinutesConcise, decisions and actions with owners and dates

Gathering and organising information

Collect facts before you write: dates, times, names, quantities, records, photos. Then organise them. Use a mind map or a simple list of points in order. For reports, group information under headings such as Background, Findings, Recommendations.

lessons.title: Drafting with clarity and correct conventions
lessons.html:
Writing clearly

Principles of plain writing

  • Put the main point first. Readers are busy.
  • Use short sentences and paragraphs with one main idea each.
  • Prefer active voice: 'The night shift cleaned the grader' rather than 'The grader was cleaned by the night shift'.
  • Use specific, concrete words: '14 cartons were underweight' rather than 'some cartons had issues'.
  • Use headings, numbered steps and bullet points to make information easy to find.
  • Be consistent with terms; do not call the same thing a 'bin' in one paragraph and a 'crate' in the next.

Conventions of common formats

Email: clear subject line, greeting, purpose in the first sentence, brief body, clear request or action, polite closing with your name and position. Reply promptly and check recipients before sending.

Memo: To, From, Date, Subject, then the message in short paragraphs.

Business letter: letterhead, date, recipient's name and address, reference, salutation, body, closing such as 'Yours faithfully' or 'Yours sincerely', signature, name and title.

Incident report: date, time, place, people involved, what happened in order, injuries or damage, immediate action taken, witnesses, signature. State facts, not blame or speculation.

Minutes: date, attendees, apologies, items discussed, decisions, actions with responsible person and due date.

Writing to persuade

When asking management for resources, structure your argument: describe the problem with evidence, propose a solution, show the costs and benefits, and state what you want approved. For example: 'Over the last month, 6% of packed cartons were rejected because of label smudging. A replacement label printer costs about R18 000. Reducing rejects by half would save more than this within the season.'

Tone

Be polite and professional, even when writing about a problem. Avoid capitals for emphasis, which reads as shouting, and avoid emotional language.

lessons.title: Editing, presenting and responsible writing
lessons.html:
Revising your writing

First drafts are rarely perfect. Set your draft aside briefly, then revise it.

Revision checklist

  1. Purpose: Does it achieve what I intended? Is the request or action clear?
  2. Audience: Will the reader understand it? Have I explained terms?
  3. Content: Are all facts, numbers, dates and names correct? Is anything missing?
  4. Structure: Is it in a logical order? Are headings helpful?
  5. Language: Are sentences clear and grammatically correct? Is the tone right?
  6. Mechanics: Spelling, punctuation, capital letters, consistent numbers and units.

Common errors to watch for

  • Run-on sentences joined with commas.
  • Confusing words such as its and it's, there and their, affect and effect.
  • Inconsistent tense: switching between past and present.
  • Missing units: write 25 kg, 4 °C, R1 200.
  • Ambiguous dates: write 3 March 2026 or use the agreed company format.

Presentation

Neat presentation makes a good impression. Use the company template, consistent fonts and spacing, and include page numbers on longer documents. Handwritten records should be legible, in pen and corrected with a single line and initials, never with correction fluid.

Responsible writing

  • Accuracy: records such as temperature logs and QC checks must reflect what really happened. Falsifying records is serious misconduct and can put consumers at risk.
  • Confidentiality: do not share personal information about workers, disciplinary matters or customer data with people who are not authorised.
  • Respect: avoid discriminatory or offensive language. Remember that emails can be forwarded and kept.
  • Records: file documents in the right place and keep them for the required period.

Key points

  • Plan purpose, audience, context and format before writing.
  • Put the main point first and use short, active, specific sentences.
  • Follow the conventions of emails, memos, letters, reports and minutes.
  • Persuade with evidence, costs and benefits.
  • Revise for content, structure, language and mechanics.
  • Write accurately, confidentially and respectfully.
